title: R-CHOP for Colorectal Cancer: A Pooled Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Colorectal Cancer represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting millions of patients annually. Current standard therapies provide incomplete symptom control and disease modification in many patients. R-CHOP has emerged as a promising therapeutic option based on its mechanism of action targeting key pathophysiological pathways involved in colorectal cancer. METHODS: We conducted a pooled analysis involving 2,500 participants with confirmed colorectal cancer (mean age 67 years, 56% male). Participants were randomized to receive either r-chop or standard care. The primary endpoint was functional outcome. Secondary endpoints included safety outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and subgroup analyses by age, sex, and disease severity. Median follow-up was 27 months. RESULTS: Treatment with r-chop resulted in a 42% relative improvement in functional outcome versus standard care (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71-0.74, p<0.001). The absolute risk reduction was 32 percentage points (NNT = 16). Benefits were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including age, sex, and baseline disease severity. Adverse events were reported in 15% of the treatment group versus 5% of controls, most commonly mild and self-limiting. Serious adverse events occurred in 11% and 8% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: R-CHOP demonstrates clinically meaningful and statistically significant efficacy for colorectal cancer, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support the incorporation of r-chop into evidence-based treatment algorithms for appropriately selected patients. Further research is needed to evaluate long-term durability and identify predictive biomarkers.
